desc: The command responsible for detecting and defeating air threats to North America, and the institution whose public statements since 2023 constitute the government's most damaging admissions on the observational record. NORAD counted more than 600 drone reports above US military installations since 2022. Its commander since February 2024, Gen. Gregory Guillot, made counter-UAS the centrepiece of a 90-day assessment driven by the Langley incursions, established the Falcon Peak counter-drone demonstration series, and stated on the record that he knew of no 'organized or unorganized foreign nexus' to Langley. In February 2023 NORAD-controlled fighters destroyed three unidentified objects over Alaska, the Yukon and Lake Huron in four days, none of which were recovered intact and two of which an allied government's own Secret memorandum described as unverified as to function and propulsion. By March 2026 Guillot confirmed detections over installations had increased year on year with roughly a quarter defeated. A homeland air defence command that cannot attribute persistent intrusions over its own bomber and fighter bases is the strongest available argument that the observational record is a live national-security problem rather than a historical curiosity.

dossier.narrative:
This node is on the map because of what its records are, not what anyone claims about it.

The 1975 material is primary and contemporaneous. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log, released over a colonel's signature and stamped as pages of a larger compilation, records calls from Strategic Air Command posts, two F-106s launched, that the fighters did not get down to the objects, and lights extinguishing on fighter arrival. The National Military Command Center memorandum of 29 October 1975 shows the traffic reaching the Chairman, the Joint Staff and the service chiefs, with a general officer personally approving rules of engagement for a National Guard helicopter.

One unresolved detail is carried openly rather than smoothed. The NORAD log names Minot Air Force Station, a radar site, where the CINCNORAD message of 11 November says Minot AFB. Those are different places and the discrepancy matters for which base a claim attaches to. Nothing opened resolves it, so the board states both and attaches the claim to neither silently.

The modern material is of a different character and is kept distinct. Drone reports over installations since 2022 are an acknowledged, funded, operational problem with named programmes attached. The board carries them because the same command is the reporter, and because a reader tracing how official language about unidentified objects has changed will want both ends of the line in one place. It does not assert that the two eras are the same phenomenon.

dossier.whatItIs: The North American Aerospace Defense Command and US Northern Command, the binational and homeland commands responsible for aerospace warning and control over North America. On this board they appear in two eras that are usually discussed separately: the 1975 northern-tier intrusions, recorded in NORAD's own regional logs, and the post-2022 drone-incursion reporting over US military installations.
dossier.whyImplicated: Because the same command's own records bracket the subject at both ends. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for November 1975 records fighters launched against objects over weapons storage areas and lights extinguishing on their arrival. Fifty years later the same command reports more than 600 drone sightings over US installations since 2022 and stands up a counter-drone demonstration programme. Whatever the objects are in either period, the institution recording them is the one whose job is knowing what is in the airspace.
